content: 1. Coomarasamy A. conducted a meta-analysis in 2011, published in the BMJ, comparing the outcomes of cesarean sections performed by clinical officers versus medical doctors in developing countries. The study analyzed controlled trials to assess differences in outcomes. 2. Colvin C., de Heer J., Winterton L., Glenton C., Lewin S., Rashidian A., and colleagues undertook a systematic review in 2012 to identify barriers and facilitators to implementing task-shifting in midwifery programs. This review was still in progress at the time. 3. Glenton C., Colvin C., Carlsen B., Swartz A., Lewin S., Noyes J., and others conducted a systematic review in 2012 to explore barriers and facilitators to implementing lay health worker programs aimed at improving maternal and child health. This review was also in progress. 4. Glenton C., Khanna R., Morgan C., and Nilsen ES. initiated a systematic review in 2012 to evaluate the effects, safety, and acceptability of compact, prefilled, auto-disable injection devices, such as Uniject™, when administered by lay health workers. This review was ongoing. 5. Gopinathan U., Lewin S., and Glenton C. began a review in 2012 to examine large-scale programs designed to scale up human resources for health in lowand middle-income countries. This study was in progress. 6. Rashidian A., Karimi-Shahanjarini A., Shakibazadeh E., Glenton C., Noyes J., Lewin S., and colleagues conducted a systematic review in 2012 to investigate barriers and facilitators affecting the effectiveness and implementation of doctor-nurse substitution programs. This review was ongoing. 7. Lewin S., Glenton C., Owolabi O., and Pakenham-Walsh N. analyzed stakeholder perspectives on optimizing the roles of healthcare providers for maternal and newborn health in lowand middle-income countries. This analysis, based on the HIFA 2015 email archive, was in progress in 2012. 8. De Savigny D. and Adam T. authored a publication in 2009 titled Systems Thinking for Health Systems Strengthening, which was released by the World Health Organization in Geneva. This work emphasizes the application of systems thinking to improve health systems. 9. Guyatt G., Oxman AD., Akl EA., Kunz R., Vist G., Brozek J., and colleagues introduced the GRADE guidelines in 2011. The guidelines provide a framework for creating evidence profiles and summary of findings tables, as published in the Journal of Clinical Epidemiology. 10. The World Health Organization (WHO) published global recommendations and guidelines on task-shifting in 2007. This document outlines the rational distribution of tasks among health workforce teams to optimize healthcare delivery. 11. WHO released recommendations in 2011 for the prevention and treatment of pre-eclampsia and eclampsia. These guidelines aim to improve maternal health outcomes globally. 12. Lavis JN., Rottingen JA., Bosch-Capblanch X., Atun R., El-Jardali F., Gilson L., and others published guidance in 2012 in PLoS Medicine. This work links evidence-informed guidance development to policy-making processes in health systems. 13. WHO issued recommendations in 2012 for the prevention and treatment of postpartum hemorrhage. These guidelines aim to address one of the leading causes of maternal mortality worldwide. 14. Lavis JN., Wilson MG., Oxman AD., Lewin S., and Fretheim A. developed SUPPORT tools for evidence-informed health policymaking. In 2009, they published a tool (STP 4) in Health Research Policy and Systems to help clarify problems using research evidence. 15. Kingdon JW. authored the second edition of Agendas, Alternatives, and Public Policies in 2003. This book explores the processes of policy-making and agenda-setting in public policy. 16. Fretheim A., Munabi-Babigumira S., Oxman AD., Lavis JN., and Lewin S. published a SUPPORT tool (STP 6) in 2009 to guide the use of research evidence in addressing how policy options will be implemented. This was featured in Health Research Policy and Systems. 17. Fretheim A., Oxman AD., Lavis JN., and Lewin S. developed another SUPPORT tool (STP 18) in 2009, focusing on planning, monitoring, and evaluating health policies. This was also published in Health Research Policy and Systems. 18. WHO maintains the Reproductive Health Library, which was updated in 2012. This resource provides evidence-based recommendations and guidelines to improve reproductive health globally.
